papers.title: Robust Harmful Features Under Jailbreak Attacks: Mechanistic Evidence from Attention Head Specialization in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment, yet their mechanisms remain poorly understood. We provide evidence that attacks do not comprehensively eliminate safety features, but instead selectively suppress specific attention heads. We identify two functionally differentiated types: Adversarially Compromised Heads (ACHs) concentrated in early layers, which are suppressed under attacks, and Safety-Aligned Heads (SAHs) in mid-layers, which maintain robust activations even when attacks succeed. Ablation studies support the causal role of ACHs and the contribution of SAHs to robust activations: suppressing a small number of ACHs is sufficient to induce jailbreak-like behavior on normally refused inputs, while removing SAHs substantially weakens mid-layer safety activations. Token-level attribution further shows that ACH suppression is driven specifically by attack-template tokens, providing a mechanistic account of why attacks can bypass refusal decisions through ACH suppression while leaving internal safety signals sustained by SAHs -- a phenomenon we term Robust Harmful Features. To validate the practical significance of this robustness, we show that simply reading these persistent activations -- without any training -- yields competitive aggregate detection performance with strong adversarial robustness.
papers.comment: 323 pages, 19 figures. Accepted at ICML 2026 as a Oral presentation

summary.takeaway: Jailbreak attacks selectively suppress specific attention heads in LLMs, revealing a nuanced mechanism of safety feature persistence.
summary.problem: The mechanisms by which jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment are poorly understood.
summary.method: The study identifies and classifies attention heads into Adversarially Compromised Heads (ACHs) and Safety-Aligned Heads (SAHs) to analyze their roles during attacks.
summary.evidence: Ablation studies demonstrate that suppressing ACHs induces jailbreak-like behavior, while SAHs maintain robust activations.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide numerical results for the competitive performance of the proposed detector on safety-eval benchmarks.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding the functional differentiation of attention heads can inform the design of more resilient LLM safety mechanisms.

papers.title: Online Data Selection for Instruction Tuning via Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: With Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training and fine-tuning shifting its focus from data volume to data quality, quality data selection has emerged as a critical research topic. Existing online data selection methods for LLM training are typically "batch-constrained", limiting optimization to local utility within random batches. To overcome this, we propose GAIA (Global Adaptive Instruction tuning via GAussian processes), a framework that formulates data valuation as a global estimation process. GAIA employs Gaussian Process regression to model continuous utility manifolds across the semantic space, utilizing an adaptive strategy fusion mechanism to dynamically prioritize high-utility samples. By casting the strategy-posterior update as an instance of the classical fixed-share Hedge framework for tracking the best expert, we inherit a dynamic-regret guarantee that characterizes GAIA's robustness under non-stationary quality scores during training. Empirical evaluations on three datasets demonstrate that GAIA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines like \greats, establishing our method as a scalable and robust solution for efficient instruction tuning.

summary.takeaway: GAIA is a novel framework for online data selection in LLM instruction tuning that enhances data quality through Gaussian Processes.
summary.problem: Existing online data selection methods are limited by batch-constrained paradigms, leading to suboptimal sample selection.
summary.method: GAIA employs Gaussian Process regression to model data utility globally, allowing for dynamic prioritization of high-utility samples.
summary.evidence: Empirical evaluations show that GAIA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines like GREATS across multiple datasets.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide specific numerical results or detailed comparisons for all baselines.
summary.why_for_you: This research is relevant for improving data selection strategies in LLMs, enhancing model performance and robustness.

signals.text: GAIA models the latent quality function over the entire training corpus using Gaussian Processes.

papers.title: ToolPrivacyBench: Benchmarking Purpose-Bound Privacy in Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have increasingly moved from standalone text generation systems to agents that invoke external tools, access environments, and execute multi-step tasks. However, conventional function-calling benchmarks mainly evaluate task completion and API correctness, while privacy evaluation benchmarks typically focus on final responses or privacy judgments. Neither perspective captures purpose-bound information flow across an executed multi-tool trajectory. Motivated by this limitation in current agent evaluation, ToolPrivacyBench audits whether task-private atoms are routed only to authorized tools and downstream sinks, thereby evaluating both task completion and privacy over-disclosure during tool use. The benchmark contains 2,150 cases, including 1,150 fully synthetic privacy-sensitive business workflows and 1,000 cases adapted from existing multi-tool and function-calling benchmarks. Each case is represented by a policy knowledge base. After an agent executes against mock business backends, the evaluator compares recorded tool arguments and backend audit logs with this policy knowledge base. The evaluation covers nine widely used agents to characterize purpose-bound privacy over-disclosure. The results show that successful tool execution does not imply appropriate privacy disclosure: an agent may complete a task while transmitting unnecessary private information through intermediate tool calls. ToolPrivacyBench therefore formalizes a need-to-know disclosure boundary, under which each tool should receive only the information necessary for its stated purpose, and uses trajectory-level auditing to identify privacy over-disclosure in multi-tool workflows.

summary.takeaway: ToolPrivacyBench evaluates purpose-bound privacy in tool-using LLM agents during multi-step workflows.
summary.problem: Existing benchmarks fail to assess privacy over-disclosure in multi-tool agent workflows.
summary.method: ToolPrivacyBench audits information flow using a policy knowledge base to ensure only necessary data is shared with tools.
summary.evidence: The benchmark includes 2,150 cases and evaluates nine widely used agents, revealing that task completion does not guarantee appropriate privacy disclosure.
summary.limitations: The study does not provide evidence on the effectiveness of privacy measures in real-world applications.
summary.why_for_you: This research is crucial for developing trustworthy LLMs that respect user privacy in complex task executions.

signals.text: Successful tool execution can still lead to unnecessary private information disclosure.
ToolPrivacyBench uses a policy knowledge base to audit privacy compliance.
The benchmark reveals high rates of privacy over-disclosure across various agents.

deep_dive.overview: ToolPrivacyBench addresses the gap in evaluating privacy in LLM agents by focusing on purpose-bound information flow during multi-tool workflows. It assesses whether agents respect need-to-know boundaries while executing tasks, highlighting the importance of privacy compliance alongside task completion.

papers.title: Low-Agreeableness Persona Conditioning for Safe LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) for social warmth degrades factual reliability and increases sycophancy. We investigate a related but distinct failure mode: warmth fine-tuning also weakens adversarial safety, making models more susceptible to jailbreaks and harmful output generation. We examine whether this reflects an inherent consequence of empathetic adaptation or an artifact of data construction. To address this, we introduce a persona-driven rewriting pipeline that conditions user turns on low agreeableness and pairs this with warm, de-escalating assistant responses. Across three experiments on four models, our approach reduces jailbreak susceptibility and harmful output rates relative to generic warmth fine-tuning baselines, while preserving conversational warmth. Representational probing provides suggestive evidence that this conditioning reduces the geometric alignment between warmth and compliance directions in latent space. These results show that safer empathetic fine-tuning is achievable through data design alone, without safety labels, harm detectors, or changes to the training objective.

summary.takeaway: Low-agreeableness persona conditioning enhances safety in LLM fine-tuning without sacrificing warmth.
summary.problem: Warmth fine-tuning in LLMs can degrade factual reliability and increase susceptibility to harmful outputs.
summary.method: A persona-driven rewriting pipeline conditions user turns on low agreeableness while pairing with warm assistant responses.
summary.evidence: Experiments show reduced jailbreak susceptibility and harmful output rates compared to generic warmth fine-tuning baselines.
summary.limitations: The study does not provide extensive evidence on the long-term effects of the proposed method.
summary.why_for_you: This research offers insights into improving LLM safety while maintaining empathetic interactions.

signals.text: Low-agreeableness conditioning reduces the geometric alignment between warmth and compliance directions.
The persona-driven rewriting pipeline does not require safety labels or harm detectors.
Fine-tuning on low-agreeableness dialogues outperforms generic warmth fine-tuning on safety metrics.

deep_dive.overview: The paper investigates the trade-off between warmth and safety in LLM fine-tuning, proposing a novel approach that conditions user interactions on low agreeableness to enhance adversarial safety while preserving conversational warmth.

papers.title: Reward-Free Code Alignment from Pretrained or Fine-Tuned LLM: Unpacking the Trade-offs for Code Generation
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) alignment trains an LLM using preference data to produce outputs that better meet established quality standards. While LLM alignment techniques are studied for non-coding tasks, we know little about their usefulness for coding tasks. It is unclear whether LLM code alignment could support both functional requirements (producing executable, correct code) and non-functional requirements (code readability, style, maintainability). It is also unknown whether alignment for a code LLM should begin with base pretrained version or the finetuned (i.e., instruction-tuned) version of the LLM. In this paper, we offer insights on the above two research questions by conducting an empirical study. We studied five state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs using two widely used LLM alignment techniques: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and BoNBoN. For each training record, we created a preference pair as accepted and rejected instances by using the SelfCodeAlign pipeline. DPO and BoNBoN are reward-free models, i.e., they eliminate the need for multiple reward scores for output preferences. We tuned each LLM using the two alignment techniques in two settings: pretrained and finetuned versions of an LLM. We evaluated functional requirements using four SOTA benchmarks (HumanEval+, MBPP+, EvalPerf, EvoEval) and non-functional requirements using the CODAL benchmark, which evaluates code quality across five dimensions derived from software engineering practices. We find that pretrained-to-aligned pathways achieve larger improvements in the aligned variant over its pretrained variant. But the pretrained variant is generally less accurate than its finetuned variant. However, finetuned- to-aligned offers smaller performance improvements or, in some cases, degradation in the aligned variant than its finetuned variant.
papers.journal_ref: The ACM International Conference on the Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE) 2026

summary.takeaway: LLM alignment techniques can enhance code generation quality but show varying effectiveness based on model type and alignment pathway.
summary.problem: The effectiveness of LLM alignment for coding tasks, particularly regarding functional and non-functional requirements, is not well understood.
summary.method: The study evaluates five SOTA LLMs using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and BoNBoN alignment techniques across pretrained and finetuned models.
summary.evidence: Pretrained-to-aligned models showed larger improvements in non-functional requirements, while finetuned-to-aligned models had smaller or negative performance changes.
summary.limitations: The study does not explore the long-term impacts of alignment on model performance beyond the immediate evaluation metrics.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding the trade-offs in LLM alignment can inform better practices for developing trustworthy code generation systems.

signals.text: Pretrained-to-aligned models achieved significant improvements, with CodeLlama-7b showing +75% in non-functional requirements.
DPO and BoNBoN are reward-free alignment techniques that optimize model outputs based on preference data.
Finetuned-to-aligned models often resulted in smaller performance gains or degradation compared to their finetuned variants.

deep_dive.overview: This paper investigates the effectiveness of LLM alignment techniques for code generation, focusing on the trade-offs between using pretrained versus finetuned models. The authors conducted empirical studies using two alignment methods, DPO and BoNBoN, across five state-of-the-art LLMs, revealing that alignment can improve non-functional code quality more consistently than functional correctness.

methodology.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
methodology.detail: DPO directly optimizes preferences using a single-stage approach, treating alignment as a classification problem without requiring a separate reward model.

methodology.title: BoNBoN
methodology.detail: BoNBoN eliminates inference-time sampling costs by training models to mimic the best-of-n distribution, combining supervised fine-tuning with iterative preference optimization.

experiments.title: Evaluation of Functional Requirements
experiments.detail: Models were evaluated using benchmarks such as HumanEval+, MBPP+, EvalPerf, and EvoEval.

experiments.title: Evaluation of Non-Functional Requirements
experiments.detail: The CODAL benchmark was used to assess code quality across five dimensions derived from software engineering practices.

findings.title: Pretrained vs. Finetuned Alignment
findings.detail: Pretrained-to-aligned pathways showed larger improvements in non-functional requirements, while finetuned-to-aligned pathways often resulted in smaller or negative performance changes.

findings.title: Model Family-Specific Preferences
findings.detail: Different models exhibited specific preferences for alignment techniques, with MetaLlama performing better with DPO and deepseek models with BoNBoN.

contributions: Provides empirical insights into the effectiveness of LLM alignment techniques for code generation.
Identifies the importance of prioritizing non-functional requirements in code alignment.
Offers recommendations for practitioners on aligning code LLMs based on empirical findings.
limitations: The study does not address the long-term effects of alignment on model performance.
Limited exploration of the generalizability of findings across different coding tasks and environments.

papers.title: SrDetection: A Self-Referential Framework for Data Leakage Detection in Code Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Evaluating code large language models (Code LLMs) requires reliable detection of data leakage, where benchmark performance is artificially inflated by exposure to benchmark data during pre-training. Existing approaches either assume access to proprietary training corpora, rely on brittle heuristics such as timestamp filtering, or use external reference sets with manually tuned, non-generalizable thresholds. To address these limitations, we introduce \textbf{SrDetection}, a unified \textbf{s}elf-\textbf{r}eferential leakage detection framework for both gray-box (access to model logits) and black-box (access to model outputs) settings. SrDetection generates semantically equivalent variants of a benchmark sample and detects leakage by contrasting the model's behavior on the original versus its variants, flagging cases where the original is disproportionately easier for the model. We further design a controlled leakage detection testbed and evaluate SrDetection in this environment. Across different models and training stages, SrDetection improves average F1 by 21.52 points in the gray-box setting and 14.46 points in the black-box setting over strong baselines, demonstrating robust, threshold-independent leakage detection. Finally, a gray-box study of 15 widely used Code LLMs on four popular benchmarks reveals benchmark-specific leakage patterns beyond prior overlap-based analyses\footnote{\footnotesize Source code and data are available at https://github.com/SMinL/SrDetectionCode

summary.takeaway: SrDetection provides a robust framework for detecting data leakage in Code LLMs without relying on external references.
summary.problem: Existing data leakage detection methods are limited by their reliance on proprietary training data or brittle heuristics.
summary.method: SrDetection contrasts model behavior on original code samples with semantically equivalent variants to detect leakage.
summary.evidence: SrDetection improves average F1 scores by 21.52 points in gray-box and 14.46 points in black-box settings over strong baselines.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed numerical results for all models and benchmarks tested.
summary.why_for_you: This framework enhances the reliability of evaluating Code LLMs, crucial for researchers focused on model performance.

signals.text: SrDetection improves F1 scores significantly across various models and training stages.
The framework operates in both gray-box and black-box settings, enhancing its applicability.
Detection is based on contrasting original samples with their variants, avoiding reliance on external thresholds.

deep_dive.overview: SrDetection is a self-referential framework designed to detect data leakage in Code LLMs by generating semantically equivalent code variants and comparing model performance on these variants. This approach addresses the limitations of existing methods that depend on external data or heuristics, providing a more reliable and robust detection mechanism.

methodology.title: Code Transformation Module
methodology.detail: Generates semantically equivalent variants of code samples through minimal, localized surface edits that preserve execution behavior.

methodology.title: Detection Score Computation
methodology.detail: In gray-box settings, it computes Perplexity (PPL) for original and variant samples; in black-box settings, it compares outputs for surface-level similarity.

experiments.title: Gray-box Performance Evaluation
experiments.detail: Achieved F1 scores of 74.76 on Qwen2.5-7B and 69.99 on LLaMA3.1-8B, outperforming all baselines.

experiments.title: Black-box Performance Evaluation
experiments.detail: F1 improved from 53.09 at 1 epoch to 82.06 at 5 epochs on Qwen2.5-7B, consistently surpassing baseline methods.

findings.title: Improved Detection Rates
findings.detail: SrDetection consistently outperformed strong baselines in both gray-box and black-box settings.

findings.title: Benchmark-specific Leakage Patterns
findings.detail: A gray-box study revealed unique leakage patterns across 15 widely used Code LLMs.

contributions: Introduction of SrDetection as a self-referential framework for sample-level leakage detection.
Development of an automatic code augmentation method that generates contrastive variants.
Creation of a controlled testbed for evaluating leakage detection across different models and benchmarks.
limitations: The paper does not provide detailed numerical results for all models and benchmarks tested.
Potential variability in performance across different datasets and model architectures is not fully explored.
